name: Responder - Passive Analysis Mode
description: Runs Responder in analyze mode (-A): listens to LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS broadcast traffic and logs who is broadcasting queries without responding. Use this first to confirm victims exist and scope the attack before going active.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== WHY LLMNR/NBT-NS POISONING WORKS ===
Windows uses three fallback name-resolution protocols when DNS fails:
  1. LLMNR  — Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (UDP 5355, multicast to 224.0.0.252)
  2. NBT-NS — NetBIOS Name Service (UDP 137, subnet broadcast)
  3. MDNS   — Multicast DNS (UDP 5353)

When a user typos a UNC path (\\FILESHRE\docs instead of \\FILESHARE), DNS fails,
so Windows broadcasts to the subnet: 'Does anyone know FILESHRE?' An attacker on the
same L2 segment replies first: 'That's me.' Windows tries to authenticate, sending
the user's NTLMv2 challenge-response to the attacker — who captures the hash.

=== WHAT ANALYZE MODE DOES ===
With -A, Responder NEVER sends any packet — it only reads. You see:
  [*] [LLMNR]   NBT-NS requests from 172.16.5.25 for name MISTYPED-HOST
  [*] [NBT-NS]  172.16.5.125 is querying for DCC01 (would respond to: 172.16.5.125)
The key word 'would' = not yet responding. This confirms which hosts are vulnerable
before creating any authentication events in Windows logs.

=== WHEN TO USE ANALYZE vs ACTIVE ===
  -A only → first 15-30 min; silent; no authentication events generated
  active  → run when you're ready to capture; creates Event ID 4625 (failed auth)
  Rule: always start passive, confirm traffic exists, then switch to active.

=== OUTPUT TO LOOK FOR ===
Look for frequency and variety of requests. Heavy LLMNR traffic = busy environment =
high probability of capturing high-privilege hashes. Service accounts often
query for printers, file servers, backup services — those are gold.

=== HASH STORAGE (when active) ===
  /usr/share/responder/logs/
  Pattern: (MODULE)-(HASHTYPE)-(CLIENT_IP).txt
  e.g.: SMB-NTLMv2-SSP-172.16.5.25.txt
  NTLMv2 ≠ pass-the-hash. Must crack offline with hashcat -m 5600.

recommended.note: Switch to active mode to capture NetNTLM hashes.

defense.why_it_works: Responder in analyze mode passively OBSERVES LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS and browser traffic without answering, to map victims and name-resolution behaviour before poisoning.
defense.prerequisites: A position on the LAN segment.
defense.impact: Reconnaissance of who is broadcasting what - targets for later poisoning - with no packets injected.
defense.detection: Passive - Responder answers nothing, so there is little to detect; the underlying LLMNR/NBT-NS chatter is what enables it.
defense.artifacts: None injected; a local capture of observed broadcasts.
defense.prevention: Disabling LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS removes the traffic to observe (and to poison); detection is otherwise infeasible for pure analyze mode.
defense.evasion: Analyze mode is passive by nature - it injects nothing and is effectively undetectable on the wire.
defense.misconfiguration: LLMNR (Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution, UDP 5355) and NBT-NS (NetBIOS Name Service, UDP 137) are enabled by default on Windows and are used as fallback name resolution when DNS fails. These protocols broadcast name queries on the local network segment. Any host on the same subnet can respond to these broadcasts — a Responder instance claims to be the queried host and captures the NTLMv2 hash when the victim tries to authenticate.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# LLMNR enabled (Windows default):
# Registry: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\DNSClient
#   EnableMulticast: (not set or 1) = LLMNR active

# NBT-NS enabled (Windows default):
# Network adapter -> TCP/IP properties -> WINS -> 'Enable NetBIOS over TCP/IP'
# = Default (or Enabled)

# Test: trigger a failed DNS lookup, watch Responder capture NTLMv2:
# net use \\nonexistent  -> host broadcasts LLMNR for 'nonexistent'
# Responder replies -> host sends NTLMv2 -> Responder captures it
defense.secure_config:
# Disable LLMNR via GPO:
# Computer Config > Admin Templates > Network > DNS Client
#   'Turn off multicast name resolution' = Enabled
# OR Registry:
Set-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\DNSClient' \
    -Name EnableMulticast -Value 0

# Disable NBT-NS via GPO (push WMI script or DHCP option 001 = 0x2):
# Or per-machine:
Get-WmiObject Win32_NetworkAdapterConfiguration | ForEach-Object {
    $_.SetTcpipNetbios(2)  # 2 = Disable NetBIOS
}

# Enable SMB signing (stops relay attacks even if hash captured):
Set-SmbServerConfiguration -RequireSecuritySignature $true -Force
